The design deliberately trades breadth for adjudicability: math + formal checking to minimize judge noise.44:T4a4,The method defines a context-conditioned risk landscape over first-token branches. For a prompt x and a candidate first token v, the evaluator forces Y1=v, then repeatedly samples the rest of the response from the second token onward under a specified decoding protocol. A jailbreak judge J labels each completed trajectory, and the branch score h_x(v) is the estimated probability of a harmful continuation given that first-token branch. Measuring h_x(v) over the top-K first-token candidates gives a continuous branch-risk landscape. DHS weights branch scores by the evaluated decoder’s first-token distribution, making it closer to operational exposure. AHS weights measured branches uniformly, describing the average risk in the inspected neighborhood. CHBR@K measures hidden basins: among prompts whose top-1 branch appears safe, it asks how often a high-risk branch appears when the neighborhood is expanded. By pairing clean and attacked landscapes, the paper separates three attack mechanisms: exploiting a pre-existing risky branch, activating risk conditionally in an existing branch, and replacing the candidate set with a harmful branch absent from the clean top candidates.45:T7e6,方法设计很克制，重点在评估协议而不是新模型。论文先把单步 repair 定义为在历史 h_t 处把原动作 a_t 替换为 a'，之后由 executor e 继续完成剩余 episode。核心目标不是 post-repair success probability，而是 net gain，也就是 p_e(h_t,a') - p_e(h_t,a_t)。这样做的原因很关键：原动作在重跑时也可能成功，如果只看修复后的成功率，会把本来就可能成功的部分也算到 repair 头上；而且不同位置的 baseline 不同，只看 post-repair success 会改变 repair 排序。

在评估协议上，作者固定三样东西：失败轨迹、候选单步 repair 集合、部署 executor e0。然后对每个候选 repair，用不参与选择的独立 rollout 估计其在 e0 下的真实净收益，作为 matched target。各类 evaluator 只负责打分和选 repair，不能使用这些独立标签。最后比较 evaluator 选中的 repair 与 matched selection 之间的 deployment value gap，也就是 decision regret。

论文考察的 evaluator 很全，包含：1）部署模型自身的 greedy replay；2）替代 executor 的 rollout，例如用更强的 Qwen2.5-14B 去评估给 7B 部署模型用的 repair；3）不同家族模型互评，如 Qwen2.5-7B 与 Llama-3.1-8B 互相为对方选 repair；4）环境 oracle；5）已有 verification rule；6）只读失败日志的 LLM judge。作者还做了 cross-fitted selection loss 和预注册分析计划，尽量避免“先看结果再挑 case”的偏差。

一个很重要的技术点是，他们不仅比较 value estimate 是否相关，还专门找 preference reversal：两个 evaluator 是否会在同一失败案例上偏好相反的 repair。新鲜 rollout 结果表明，这种 reversal 真实存在，不是估计噪声。另一个细节是，他们区分 unscreened failure pools 和 screened pools。前者不预先筛选“有修复价值”的失败，更接近真实部署；后者用于更广泛比较 evaluator，但不会掩盖主结论。46:T8a9,实验覆盖 gridworld、ALFWorld 和 WebShop，部署 agent 主要是 Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct 与 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct，Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct 作为替代 executor 之一。关键结果有几组。

1）在未筛选的失败池上，greedy replay 即使用的是部署模型自己，也会有明显损失：相对 matched selection，在 ALFWorld 上损失 0.08–0.13 的 expected net success gain，在 WebShop 上损失 0.06–0.13 的 net reward。这里说明 deterministic replay 不能替代 rollout-based deployed-policy evaluation，因为 repair 的价值来自后续随机执行分布，而不是单条贪心轨迹。

2）更强模型替代弱部署模型也会错。用 Qwen2.5-14B 的每候选 5 次 rollout 来给 Qwen2.5-7B 选 repair，在 ALFWorld 上损失 0.25，在 WebShop 上损失 0.07。这个结果很有信息量：更强 executor 的 value function 不是弱 executor 的更低噪声近似，而可能是另一个目标函数。

3）不同模型之间的错配是双向的。Qwen2.5-7B 和 Llama-3.1-8B 在两个环境里互相给对方选 repair 都会产生损失。作者进一步分析发现，Qwen-14B 与 Qwen-7B 在部分 case 上会偏好相反 repair；而 Llama 更多表现为无法把 7B 真正需要的两个 repair 拉开差距。

4）增加 substitute executor 的 rollout 数只能缓慢缩小差距。20 个 14B rollout per candidate，在 ALFWorld 上选出的 repair 价值大致只相当于 7B 自己 1 个 rollout 的效果；在 WebShop 上还不如 7B 自己 2 个 rollout。这说明“多用强模型采样”不是高效补救。

5）少量 deployed-agent verification 很有效。论文后段分析了何时瓶颈在 evaluator、何时瓶颈在 candidate set。结论是，如果候选 repair 质量尚可，给每个候选加少量部署策略 rollout，能回收大部分 regret；但如果候选集本身缺少真正有用的 repair，再好的 evaluator 也无能为力。

6）标签层面的影响也被量化。executor 的变化不仅影响 repair ranking，还会改变 repair-location label 指向哪一步，并改变 benchmark 上“哪种 repair method 排第一”。这意味着很多 repair benchmark 的标签并不是 executor-invariant 的。47:T7b7,The technical contribution is mainly an evaluation protocol rather than a new repair model. A single-step repair is defined as replacing action a_t with a' at history h_t, after which an executor e completes the rest of the episode. The primary objective is net gain, p_e(h_t, a') - p_e(h_t, a_t), rather than post-repair success probability. This choice matters: the original action may still succeed on rerun, so a repair should only get credit for the extra success it adds; also, different positions have different baselines, so post-repair success can change the ranking across repair locations.

The protocol fixes three objects: the failed trajectory, the candidate repair set, and the deployed executor e0. For every candidate repair, the authors estimate its true value under e0 using independent rollouts that are never used for selection. Each evaluator then scores candidates using its own mechanism, and the selected repair is compared against matched selection, which uses the deployed executor’s own rollouts. The gap in deployed value is the decision regret.

The evaluator set is broad: greedy replay of the deployed model, rollout-based scoring with a substitute executor such as Qwen2.5-14B, cross-model evaluation between Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B, environment oracles, published verification rules, and LLM judges that only read the failed log. The paper also uses cross-fitted selection loss and a dated analysis plan to reduce researcher degrees of freedom.

A particularly useful part is the analysis of preference reversals. The authors do not stop at showing different value estimates; they test whether different evaluators actually prefer different repairs on the same failure case. Fresh rollouts confirm that such reversals are real. Another good design choice is the separation between unscreened failure pools, which better reflect deployment, and screened pools, which allow broader evaluator comparisons without weakening the main claim.48:T864,Experiments cover a gridworld, ALFWorld, and WebShop. The deployed agents are mainly Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, with Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct used as one substitute executor. The main findings are clear.

1) On unscreened failure pools, greedy replay already incurs nontrivial loss even when the evaluator is the deployed model itself. Relative to matched selection, greedy replay loses 0.08–0.13 expected net success gain in ALFWorld and 0.06–0.13 net reward in WebShop. This shows that deterministic replay is not a reliable proxy for rollout-based deployed-policy value.

2) A stronger substitute executor can still be a poor selector. Using five Qwen2.5-14B rollouts per candidate to choose repairs for a deployed Qwen2.5-7B loses 0.25 in ALFWorld and 0.07 in WebShop. The stronger model is not simply a lower-variance estimator of the weaker model’s value function; it can optimize a meaningfully different counterfactual.

3) Mismatch is bidirectional across model families. Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B both incur loss when selecting repairs for each other in both environments. The follow-up analysis is informative: Qwen-14B and Qwen-7B sometimes prefer opposite repairs, while Llama more often fails to separate the repairs that the 7B executor actually needs.

4) More substitute rollouts close the gap slowly. Twenty 14B rollouts per candidate produce repairs worth roughly as much to the 7B executor as one of its own rollouts in ALFWorld, and less than two of its own in WebShop. So brute-force sampling from a stronger substitute is not an efficient fix.

5) A small amount of deployed-agent verification recovers most of the loss. The later sections analyze when the bottleneck is evaluator mismatch and when it is the candidate set itself. If the candidate set already contains useful repairs, a few deployed-policy rollouts per candidate recover much of the regret; if not, better evaluation alone cannot help.

6) The mismatch also affects labels and benchmark rankings. Changing the executor changes not only repair values but also repair-location labels and which repair method appears best on a benchmark.49:T419,Start with the introduction and problem setup. Two definitions are central: net gain instead of post-repair success, and matched selection as the reference point. Those choices determine the entire evaluation logic.

Then read the main experimental sections, especially the unscreened-pool results. Focus on three things: the size of the loss from greedy replay, the failure of stronger-model evaluation such as 14B selecting for 7B, and the fresh-rollout disagreement cases that establish genuine preference reversals rather than estimation noise.

Section 6 is worth careful reading if you care about process labels, repair supervision, or benchmark construction, because it shows that labels themselves are executor-dependent. Section 7 is the engineering section: when deployed-policy verification is cheap enough, how many rollouts are needed, and when the real bottleneck shifts to candidate generation. A quick read takes about 25–35 minutes; a deeper read should include the appendix on alternative objectives and the statistical protocol.4a:T4fc,The paper formalizes executable prefixes and defines a set of metrics.
- A rollout is a tool-invocation sequence τ̂=(a1,…,aT) executed over evolving environment states st.
- An action is executable if: the tool exists, arguments match the schema, explicit preconditions hold, cross-step data dependencies are satisfied (e.g., using an ID returned earlier), and the current environment state permits the action.
- Prefix executability checks whether each prefix (a1…ak) remains executable; aggregating over k yields a survival-style curve.
- Metrics:
  - PEC (Prefix Executability Curve): executability rate as a function of prefix length.
  - FED (First-Error Depth): the step index of the first non-executable action.
  - TER (Trajectory Executability Rate): fraction of fully executable trajectories.
  - Horizon-normalized AUC-PEC: area under PEC for length-normalized comparison.
  - RR (Recovery Rate): whether trajectories recover after entering a failure regime.
- A minimal Dual-Loop planner–verifier is used as a controlled probe (not the main contribution) to demonstrate that terminal-success rankings can diverge from prefix-executability rankings, and that pre-execution validation can improve executability metrics even when final success changes little.4b:T442,The paper introduces Visual Commission Bench with 600 tasks across 12 categories and three tiers. The Specific-Capability tier isolates reasoning, planning, long-context information extraction, and retrieval. The Multi-Stage tier examines iterative editing, visual goal interpretation, diagnosis and repair, and evidence synthesis. The Commission-Level tier covers complete visual commissions such as visual argumentation, example-driven transfer, scientific visualization, and workspace-based design. Evaluation is based on submitted artifacts, without prescribing the agent’s internal workflow. The benchmark uses 5,039 requirement checks and separates requirement fulfillment from visual quality ratings. The paper also proposes V-Protocol as a reference agent. It dynamically composes task, cognitive, and expression modules: task modules specify deliverables and dependencies, cognitive modules derive content from source materials, and expression modules produce layout and rendering specifications. A shared harness manages stage transitions, tool execution, and completion checks.4c:T566,The technical contribution is mainly a clean formalization. The paper separates the actor from the critic and grader. Under Pass@K, the actor samples K candidates independently from the original prompt. Under Seq@K, attempt t is conditioned on the interaction history, including previous outputs and feedback messages. So both metrics ask whether the task is solved within a budget of K attempts, but they probe different capabilities: independent coverage versus conditional refinement.

The paper goes beyond the metric definition by varying the feedback mode. Feedback can come from verifiers, rubric-based critiques, and different levels of error specificity. The way prior history is retained also matters. An important framing choice is that Seq@K is not meant to be a full multi-turn agent benchmark. It intentionally isolates refinement from feedback, rather than mixing it with planning, tool use, or long-horizon exploration. That isolation is useful because many existing multi-turn benchmarks entangle too many abilities at once.

Methodologically, the paper turns an often informal notion—'this model improves when corrected'—into a reproducible protocol. It also makes a useful distinction between two improvement routes: increasing first-try accuracy and increasing recovery after failure. Pass@K is more sensitive to the former; Seq@K is designed for the latter.4d:T6bc,The evaluation spans seven benchmarks across coding, complex instruction following, domain reasoning, and medical tasks, including MBPP Pro, HumanEval Pro, AdvancedIF, CLBench DKR, and HealthBench.

The first main result is that model rankings change. Some models look strong under Pass@K but gain little under sequential feedback, suggesting good first-shot performance but weak revision ability. Others are less dominant initially yet improve more reliably after feedback, making them more attractive in interactive deployment. The paper also studies cost frontiers and shows that the preferred model can change once sequential correction is allowed.

The second result is behavioral. Models differ in when they improve: some gain mostly on the first retry, while others improve later. More importantly, revisions are often poor in specific ways. Some models barely change their answer. Others address the explicit critique but break requirements that had already been satisfied. This is a useful diagnosis because it shows that 'responding to feedback' and 'repairing without regression' are distinct skills.

The third result is about the feedback itself. Informative feedback helps unevenly depending on both the benchmark and the model. Critiques written with access to the grading rubric tend to repair more failed requirements than generic feedback. Compressing prior attempts into summaries can reduce success, which means the history-retention protocol should be reported alongside Seq@K. The excerpt provided does not include full numeric tables, so the safe takeaway is structural rather than quantitative: the paper studies model selection, cost, revision behavior, and feedback design in one coherent protocol.4e:T4e1,Rubricon represents a rubric as a set of weighted binary criteria. Each criterion is a natural-language pass/fail requirement, and a verifier model evaluates whether a response satisfies it. The final response score is a normalized weighted sum. The method optimizes for three properties: discrimination, coverage, and headroom. The pipeline has three stages. Generate-and-Select samples multiple candidate rubrics and selects the one with stronger empirical separation between stronger-model and weaker-model responses, measured through criterion pass rates and the strong–weak edge. Add introduces new criteria for overlooked task requirements or observed response flaws. Prune removes criteria that are misaligned, too shallow, trivially satisfied, or unreliable for a verifier to judge. The paper also specifies criteria-writing principles: criteria should be clear, self-contained, atomic, objectively checkable, and free of cross-references. Importance labels are mapped to weights, with Critical, Major, and Minor assigned 5, 3, and 1. The key difference from self-critique, ensembling, agentic rubric generation, and Recursive Rubric Decomposition is that Rubricon uses observed scoring behavior on example responses as an external signal.4f:T5b8,The method has two main components. The first is a formalization: red-team auditing is cast as an MDP where the state is the conversation prefix, the action is the auditor’s next user turn, the transition is the target model’s stochastic reply, and the reward is the LLM-judge score for the target behavior. This separates the search algorithm from the scoring heuristic and makes it natural to compare different search strategies over the same implicit conversation tree. The second component is the introduction of value probes as branch-ranking heuristics. The authors collect judge scores on nodes from audit rollouts, back them up with discount factor gamma = 0.9, and use those backed-up targets as supervision for a linear probe over mean-pooled activations from a single layer of the target model. During auditing, this learned value estimate is used inside a beam-search harness to rank prefixes that are likely to lead to high future judge scores. The practical appeal is that the probe is much cheaper than repeated LLM-based evaluation, and the paper further argues that probes can be trained from off-policy data and even from smaller models before auditing the target model itself. Relative to prior tree-search work over LM outputs, the novelty here is that the search space is adversarial multi-turn dialogue rather than reasoning traces, and the heuristic comes from the audited model’s internal state rather than an external self-evaluator.50:T6a1,The method has three stages.
First is autoformalization. Natural-language policy statements are translated into a symbolic representation, using first-order logic or Boolean constraints that are expressive enough to support formal reasoning over obligations, permissions, prohibitions, and eligibility conditions. The goal is not maximal logical sophistication, but a stable and checkable representation that can be enumerated.
Second, the formalized rules are converted into decision trees. Branches correspond to truth assignments over atomic facts, and each path incrementally specifies a scenario. If a path is sufficient to entail the target verdict, it becomes a determined-verdict benchmark item. If the path stops before the verdict is entailed, it becomes an abstention item. This is an important design choice: it separates false from underdetermined, rather than collapsing everything into a simple entailment-versus-non-entailment setup.
Third, benchmark generation is parameterized. The system can control path depth, diversity, and target verdict types, allowing a single policy document to produce combinatorially many benchmark instances. Labels come from symbolic deduction rather than manual annotation, which is the main reason the pipeline scales while preserving correctness.
The design choice is sensible. Why formalize first instead of asking an LLM to paraphrase policies and another LLM to write questions? Because free-form generation makes label reliability fragile, especially when policies contain exceptions, interacting clauses, or missing conditions. DeoGen trades some linguistic naturalness for a much stronger guarantee on logical consistency and label validity.51:T532,DeoGen is run on four policy sources: sections of the U.S. IRS tax code, an insurance cafeteria plan, a code of coverage, and a faculty hiring handbook. From these, the system generates 451,047 benchmark entries. For evaluation, the authors sample 1,639 items and test frontier models including Claude Sonnet 5 and GPT-5.5, along with open models such as Qwen3.6 and Gemma 4.
The main results split cleanly into two regimes. When the facts determine a verdict, model correctness ranges from 75.1% to 92.5%. That is decent but far from solved, especially for regulated workflows. When the facts are insufficient and the correct behavior is to abstain, performance drops sharply to 4.0%–40.0%. This gap is the central empirical result of the paper. It suggests the main weakness is not only rule application, but failure to withhold judgment under logical underdetermination.
A second important result is the generation scale itself: four policy documents yield more than 450k benchmark items, which supports the claim that formalize-then-enumerate is a practical route to scalable deontic evaluation. If the full paper includes breakdowns by policy type, path depth, or verdict class, those are the tables worth reading, because they can help separate failures due to long rule chains, exceptions, or generic non-abstention bias.52:T8a5,The core artifact is EnvOS, a framework for task construction, pre-run certification, and post-run auditing. It starts with a phenomenon, an application-independent class of environment changes. A concrete instance is implemented as an executable perturbation with four explicit components: a state operator, a triggering condition, an observation channel, and a single-execution guard. A candidate evaluation artifact then consists of a seeded world, the perturbation, endpoint criteria, and a verifier. Crucially, this artifact is not used immediately. It is admitted only after scoped certification tests.

From the full-text description, those tests cover at least five properties: whether the state transition actually occurs; whether observations are delivered consistently to the policy; whether the task remains feasible after the change; whether the checker discriminates correct from incorrect behavior; and whether the checker is robust to corrupted or abnormal records. This is the main methodological move: benchmark construction is tied to executable certification rather than assumed validity.

A second important design choice is to separate world-state change from information disclosure. In both clinic booking and insurance approval, the authoritative state changes in all principal comparisons. What varies is what the agent sees at review time. In the clinic setting, OFF-A gives no extra review information, CUE-A gives a reminder plus a link to the original source, and LIVE-A directly shows the updated location. In insurance, OFF-A is no extra policy exposure and ON-A re-exposes the current policy at approval time. This means the experiments estimate review-information effects within a dynamic environment, rather than conflating multiple factors in a static-vs-dynamic comparison.

The evaluation pipeline also includes preregistered counting rules, isolation between policy and evaluator data, and independent re-checking of verdicts from archived evidence. That last step is especially important: the grader is no longer a single trusted endpoint, but an auditable component. For RL settings with verifiable rewards, this is effectively an audit layer on top of the reward pipeline.53:T694,The available full-text excerpt provides mostly qualitative findings and relative comparisons rather than a complete numeric table, but the experimental structure is clear. EnvOS is instantiated in two applications: clinic booking, where a session location changes mid-task, and insurance-claim approval, where a policy limit changes before the agent computes an approval amount. In both cases, the environment-side change is present; the main comparison is how much updated information is shown at review time.

Three findings stand out. First, in clinic booking, directly showing the updated location in LIVE-A outperforms merely prompting the agent to verify via a source link in CUE-A, and this remains true after paper-wide multiplicity correction. That is an informative result: explicit re-exposure of the current authoritative value helps more than a generic verification cue. Second, in insurance approval, Opus 5 succeeds on the tested silent-change instances, while Sonnet 5 shows a local benefit from policy re-exposure that does not survive the retrospective paper-wide multiplicity adjustment. Third, the authors run archive challenges with deliberately corrupted records to test whether the same pipeline can detect evidence-chain failures. Misses are reported as qualifications on the claims rather than hidden.

The most important experimental contribution is not a model ranking. The paper is careful not to pool heterogeneous conditions into a single leaderboard-style comparison. Instead, it demonstrates that without certification of intervention validity and evaluation validity, many conclusions about agent behavior in dynamic environments are not trustworthy.54:T507,This is a skim paper, but the framework is worth understanding. Adding external knowledge raises confabulation mitigation to roughly 20%. First, the authors analyze failed trajectories from SLMs and frontier models using a shared failure taxonomy. This establishes that the dominant failure modes are similar across tiers—step repetition, weak verification, and specification violations—so the gap is mostly quantitative rather than qualitative. Second, they evaluate the three capability axes separately. For solvability, they use repeated sampling and report pass@k, with each attempt executed in a fresh environment and judged by the task verifier. For verification, they study outcome verification: given a pool of completed candidate trajectories, the model must select a successful one. For confidence, the model sees only the task description and outputs a verbalized probability of success, which is evaluated with overconfidence and Brier score. A useful detail is the distinction between process verification during execution and outcome verification after generation; the main verification experiment targets the latter. The contribution is therefore a capability decomposition and evaluation protocol, not a new training method.57:T452,The key results come from OpenThoughts-TBLite and Terminal-Bench 2.1. This suggests that SLMs often can solve the task but do so unreliably. For counting, the authors define three overlap regimes across views: complete overlap, subset overlap, and complementary views. The first two can often be solved by simple per-view heuristics such as taking the maximum count. Complementary views cannot: the model must determine which detections correspond to the same physical object and which are unique, so cross-view deduplication becomes necessary.

For cross-view consistency, the benchmark avoids a naive “spot the difference” setup. Instead, it introduces localized edits either in regions visible from both viewpoints or in regions visible from only one viewpoint. Only the former creates a true contradiction. This tests whether the model reasons about visibility and shared evidence, rather than merely detecting image-level differences.

A third task, multi-view spatial reasoning, asks models to infer physical proximity relations by combining evidence across viewpoints. The dataset is built from real-world multi-view captures from DL3DV-10K and manually verified. The paper also adds diagnostic analyses: attribution to simple aggregation strategies, sensitivity to image order, no-image bias checks, explicit reasoning prompts, and scaling with additional views. These analyses make the benchmark useful for failure diagnosis, not just ranking.5a:T57e,The evaluation covers 12 open-weight and proprietary VLMs under an open-ended protocol. The clearest result appears in counting. Accuracy is relatively moderate on complete overlap, around 45.5%–81.5%, and on subset overlap, around 26.7%–76.7%. But on complementary views, where true cross-view integration is required, performance drops sharply to 4.5%–50.0%. This gap strongly suggests that many models do not reliably establish object correspondence across views.

The consistency task is even more revealing. Accuracy stays around 50%, essentially chance level, and models respond similarly to edits in shared regions and view-specific regions. That means they are often detecting differences without understanding whether those differences are compatible with two views of the same scene.

The auxiliary analyses add useful detail. A substantial fraction of counting outputs can be explained by simple per-view aggregation rules, indicating shortcut behavior. Sensitivity to image order suggests unstable multi-image fusion. Performance under reduced or removed visual input reveals language prior bias. Explicit reasoning prompts help only marginally, which implies the bottleneck is not merely missing chain-of-thought at decoding time; it is more likely a representational failure to bind observations into a coherent scene model. Adding more views does not consistently fix the issue either.5b:T8b7,方法名是 DiFuse。整体框架很克制：冻结 diffusion 和视觉编码器，不引入外部生成器，也不加辅助损失，只在 supervised fine-tuning 阶段把原生 DiT 的中间特征注入理解路径。

具体做法分三步。

第一步是特征选择。作者先做 layer-wise analysis，研究 diffusion branch 在不同层、不同去噪阶段产生的表示，哪些对空间推理最有信息量，哪些注入后对原有语义路径干扰最小。这个分析是方法成立的前提，因为 diffusion 表示不是越多越好：早期层可能过于局部、后期层可能更偏生成目标，错误选择会把噪声或无关细节带进理解分支。

第二步是空间对齐与投影。DiFuse 从 UMM 原生 DiT 中抽取中间 spatial diffusion features，把它们投影到多模态 decoder 的 hidden space，并与视觉 token 保持空间对应关系。论文反复强调 spatial correspondence，因为作者的假设不是“扩散特征提供额外语义”，而是它们提供局部结构线索。如果在 token 对齐时打乱空间位置，收益会明显下降，这一点后面也被 feature shuffling 实验证实。

第三步是注入方式。作者不是直接替换视觉 token，也不是全层强融合，而是在选定的 decoder 层通过 residual adapters 把 diffusion 特征加到 visual-token states 上。这样做的目的，是把 diffusion 表示当作补充通道，而不是主导通道，尽量避免破坏原有 semantic pathway。论文特别关心 injection position：注入太早可能扰乱语义建模，太晚则来不及影响推理。作者通过系统分析找到干扰较小、收益较高的层位。

从方法取舍上看，DiFuse 和几类相关路线有明显区别。它不同于外接 geometry module 的方法，因为没有单独结构分支；不同于 auxiliary generation/reconstruction objective，因为没有额外训练目标；也不同于 test-time 先生成再理解的 pipeline，因为它直接复用 native diffusion states，而不是把生成过程当中间步骤。它更像一种表示重用与接口设计问题：在统一模型内部，把原本只服务生成的中间状态变成理解时可调用的结构先验。5c:T990,DiFuse is deliberately lightweight. The diffusion branch and visual encoder are kept frozen. No external generator is introduced, and no auxiliary loss is added. During supervised fine-tuning, intermediate features from the model’s native diffusion transformer are injected into the understanding pathway.

The method has three main components.

First, feature selection. The authors perform a systematic layer-wise analysis over diffusion representations from different layers and denoising stages. The goal is to identify which states are informative for spatial reasoning and which can be integrated with minimal disruption to the original semantic pathway. This matters because diffusion features are not uniformly useful: some may be too local, some too generation-specific, and naive fusion can easily inject noise.

Second, spatial alignment and projection. DiFuse extracts intermediate spatial features from the native DiT, projects them into the hidden space of the multimodal decoder, and aligns them with visual tokens while preserving spatial correspondence. This is central to the paper’s hypothesis. The benefit is not supposed to come from generic extra capacity, but from transferring local structural cues. If spatial correspondence is broken, the gains should disappear, and the paper later tests exactly that.

Third, injection via residual adapters. Instead of replacing visual tokens or performing heavy fusion throughout the network, the method injects diffusion features into visual-token states at selected decoder layers using residual adapters. This treats diffusion states as a complementary channel rather than a dominant one, helping preserve the original semantic pathway. Injection position is a major design variable: too early may interfere with semantic abstraction, too late may be too weak to affect reasoning. The paper uses empirical analysis to find favorable insertion points.

Relative to related work, DiFuse differs from geometry-augmented multimodal models because it does not add a dedicated structural module; it differs from auxiliary generation/reconstruction approaches because it does not change the training objective; and it differs from generate-then-reason pipelines because it directly reuses native diffusion states rather than using generation as an intermediate procedure. The method is best understood as an interface design for internal representation transfer within a unified model.5d:T82d,Experiments are centered on UniWorld-V1, with transfer validation on OmniGen2. The main result is that DiFuse consistently improves spatial reasoning over a matched SFT baseline while keeping general multimodal performance broadly comparable.

The empirical evidence is organized around four themes.

First, main-task improvements. The paper reports gains on spatially grounded reasoning tasks after adding DiFuse. The excerpt provided does not include exact numbers, so the tables in the full paper are needed for precise margins, but the qualitative claim is clear: the spatial gains are not obtained by obviously sacrificing broad multimodal competence.

Second, ablations on feature and layer selection. The authors compare diffusion features from different layers, different denoising stages, and different decoder injection positions. This is one of the most important parts of the paper because it answers which diffusion states are actually useful. The results indicate that usefulness is selective rather than monotonic: not every layer helps, and there is a clear sweet spot for injection.

Third, tests of spatial correspondence. Feature shuffling or position perturbation substantially weakens or removes the gains, showing that the improvement depends on preserving alignment between diffusion features and visual tokens. This supports the claim that the transferred signal is structural and spatial, not just an extra source of generic features.

Fourth, transfer across architectures. Similar trends on OmniGen2 suggest that the effect is not a one-off trick tied to a single model, but a more general property of unified architectures with native diffusion branches.

For a foundation-model reader, the most useful aspect is the experimental logic. The paper does not treat diffusion features as a black-box add-on; it uses layer selection, injection-position studies, and shuffling controls to argue that native generative states carry reusable spatial structure. Exact benchmark names, training settings, and numerical gains should be checked in the full tables and appendix.5e:T43f,This is a skim-to-light-read paper. Focus on the motivation and the ablations.

1) Ask both individual-judgment questions and exact-answer questions on the same underlying objects, enabling within-family comparisons.
2) Add consistency checks across questions (e.g., compare “most common colors” against the model’s own reported color distribution), plus a control where the model is given its own counts as text to isolate reasoning/consistency from visual readout.

Metrics include exact match, MAE/RMSE for numeric errors, and P/R/F1 for binary tasks, plus best-constant baselines.61:T53f,Localization-Head Alignment (LHA) has three key pieces:
1) Identify localization heads: within Qwen3.5-4B’s full-attention layers (128 heads), find a small subset that performs evidence selection. Causal importance is validated via head ablations (ablating four localization heads hurts much more than four random heads).
2) Supervise at fact tokens inside the chain: instead of supervising attention at the final answer, apply supervision at the token positions where the model states a visual fact (e.g., when predicting the object word in “the kite is blue”). This matches the observation that perception happens when facts are written, and that attention fades later.
3) Contrastive box-based attention loss: using grounding boxes, train those heads to attend more to the evidence region than to an equal-area background. The loss is formulated as an evidence-vs-background ratio so the softmax normalizer cancels, emphasizing where attention goes rather than how much total visual attention is used.
The same auxiliary loss is used in both SFT (on the model’s own correct trajectories) and GRPO-style outcome RL (on correct rollouts). A gradient decomposition is used to argue outcome rewards select trajectories, while the attention term provides a consistent routing gradient. Inference is unchanged (no extra zoom/crop passes).62:T568,Backbone: Qwen3.5-4B in thinking mode (32K token budget, temperature 1). Diagnostics:
- Evidence masking: masking the ground-truth region costs 22.1 points more than masking an equal-area distractor region; the smaller the evidence, the larger the drop.
- Localization heads are causal: ablating four localization heads causes an additional 13.2-point drop vs ablating four random heads; their evidence focus decays with longer reasoning.

- LHA reaches 76.6% overall (Figure 1), the best single-pass Qwen3.5-4B variant in their comparison.

- Controlled gains: on identical self-generated trajectories, alignment SFT improves +1.4 over CE-SFT; after identical outcome RL, the gap grows to +1.8 (95% CI [0.5, 2.9]). Adding the attention term during RL yields an additional +0.9.
Efficiency: SFT updates only 2.6% of the LM; aligned policies produce 19% shorter rollouts (15% faster RL steps) and use 24% fewer reasoning tokens at inference. Transfer: +2.5 points on direct-answer Qwen2.5-VL-3B.63:T7e9,The method is built around three levels of unification.

First, representation unification. The paper introduces an Everything-as-RGB scheme: depth, embodiment segmentation, and first-frame-relative 2D flow are each mapped into a three-channel image-like sequence. These are then encoded by the same frozen video autoencoder used for RGB video. The motivation is straightforward: reuse the pretrained video latent space instead of introducing modality-specific encoders and decoders. The trade-off is that non-RGB modalities are forced through an RGB-like interface, so the burden is on experiments to show that important geometric structure is preserved.

Second, architectural unification. A shared Video DiT backbone handles all modalities, with lightweight task modulation providing task-specific conditioning. The transformer blocks and decoder remain shared, and the design explicitly avoids modality-specific output heads. Compared with standard multi-task systems, this is a stronger form of parameter sharing. The upside is tighter cross-task coupling and less architectural fragmentation. The downside is a higher risk of task interference, especially because generation and perception may prefer different internal representations.

Third, objective-space unification. All tasks are trained in a common velocity prediction space, following the native v-prediction formulation of diffusion models. Instead of attaching separate regression or classification heads for perception, the model learns all modalities through the same denoising-style prediction framework. At inference time, the model supports two modes: iterative future video generation with aligned dense outputs, and single-step dense perception from an observed video without full denoising rollout.

The important point is that the paper is not merely doing multi-task learning on top of a video generator. It is trying to show that generation and perception can coexist inside one shared latent dynamics model, with a common prediction formulation.64:T651,From the provided full-text excerpt, the evaluation spans diverse embodied settings, including multiple robot embodiments, human-hand interactions, and unseen tasks. The paper claims strong performance in both future video generation and dense perception, together with systematic design ablations. The excerpt does not include the full numerical tables, so the exact gains cannot be quoted here, but the experimental structure is still clear.

The first goal is to test whether joint modeling improves over a generate-then-estimate pipeline, especially in alignment and temporal consistency of dense outputs. The second is to verify that the three-way unification matters: shared backbone versus modality-specific heads, unified velocity prediction versus separate task objectives, and lightweight modulation versus more fragmented architectures. The third is to confirm that the same model is useful in both inference regimes: multi-step future imagination and single-step perception on observed videos.

The main empirical claim is reciprocal transfer. Video generation contributes strong spatiotemporal priors that help dense perception, while supervision from geometry, semantics, and motion pushes the shared backbone toward more physically meaningful representations. When reading the full paper, the most informative ablations to inspect are the ones that remove task modulation, reintroduce separate heads, or replace the unified velocity objective with task-specific losses. Those are the experiments that reveal whether the gains truly come from unification rather than from simply adding more supervision.65:T601,The technical contribution has three layers. First, the paper reframes the notion of knowledge in OPD. Standard OPD samples trajectories from the student and minimizes reverse KL to a frozen teacher at every token. Existing analyses mostly track Overlap@k, the agreement between student and teacher top-k token sets, which captures only how to branch. The authors introduce entropy shape: the sequence of next-token entropies along a trajectory. High-entropy positions correspond to forks where the model keeps options open; low-entropy positions correspond to committed continuation. This gives a concrete representation of where to branch. Second, they define Entropy Shape Correlation (ESC), which measures alignment between student and teacher entropy shapes on the same trajectory. ESC is about the positional pattern of uncertainty, not token identity. Third, they provide both observational and causal evidence that this signal matters. Observationally, in successful OPD runs, ESC rises during training together with student performance; in unsuccessful runs, ESC starts high and quickly plateaus, suggesting little remaining uncertainty gap to learn from. Causally, they build counterfactual teachers by transplanting the entropy shape of one teacher onto another while preserving token preferences as much as possible. This isolates where to branch from how to branch. The resulting experiments show that a successful teacher’s entropy shape alone can improve distillation, and that ESC can change independently of Overlap@k.66:T59f,The experiments are designed to validate mechanism rather than maximize benchmark scores. First, the authors test whether OPD gains simply come from the teacher solving more training problems. The answer is no: gains are largely unaffected by whether the teacher is correct on those specific trajectories, which suggests that the student is learning a general reasoning behavior rather than just answer knowledge. Second, in training dynamics, successful OPD runs show a steady increase in ESC alongside student improvement, while failed runs begin with high ESC and saturate early, with limited downstream gain. This is an important result because it turns “distillability” into an observable quantity. Third, the counterfactual-teacher experiments are the strongest part of the paper: by transplanting entropy shape, the authors show that changing the uncertainty pattern alone can change distillation outcomes, even when token preferences remain largely fixed. ESC can move independently of Overlap@k, supporting the claim that it is not a byproduct of token overlap. Finally, in the teacher-selection setup, pre-OPD ESC outperforms baselines based on teacher size, teacher raw performance, and Overlap@k. It ranks candidate teachers more accurately and selects the best teacher for both students under evaluation. The paper emphasizes rank correlation and regret of the selected teacher rather than only absolute downstream scores.67:T49e,This one deserves a careful read. First, example selection. EVAN estimates scaled image information gain (scaled-IIG) for each training instance, measuring how much the image contributes to answer correctness. Only visually dependent examples are selected for intervention, which avoids injecting noise into cases that can already be solved from language alone. To prevent the selected pool from collapsing into a narrow subset of tasks, the paper uses a mixed-ranking strategy that balances visual dependence with data diversity.

Second, evidence ablation. For each selected example, the method identifies query-critical image patches that support the verified response. These patches are then masked to create an evidence-ablated image. The key design choice is that the perturbation is not coarse or task-agnostic; it removes exactly the visual evidence that keeps the answer grounded. Sampling from the current policy on this ablated image tends to produce responses that remain fluent and plausible, but are now visually ungrounded. These become EVAN’s hard negatives.

Third, RL optimization. The negatives are not optimized under the ablated image. Instead, they are brought back under the clean image condition, so the model is explicitly trained to suppress language-prior failures when the relevant evidence is actually available. The training recipe includes several stabilization mechanisms: filtering out low-probability or overly long ablated responses, bounding negative advantages so negatives do not dominate the update, and combining the method with DAPO-style clipping and dynamic sampling for stable long-form reasoning optimization. Compared with prior multimodal RL methods that use image perturbations, the main difference is that EVAN treats perturbation as a tool for constructing informative negatives, not as the end objective.69:T5fe,The experimental story is not just about end-task accuracy; it is also about grounding behavior. On a set of challenging multimodal reasoning benchmarks, EVAN improves over standard RLVR/GRPO baselines, with larger gains on subsets where visual evidence is more necessary. That pattern matches the method design: it is meant to correct language shortcuts, not to uniformly help every example.

The ablations are the most informative part. Removing scaled-IIG-based selection and applying evidence ablation to all samples hurts performance, showing that visually dependent example selection is necessary. Replacing query-critical masking with random masking or coarse perturbations produces weaker negatives and worse downstream gains, which supports the claim that negative quality matters more than perturbation quantity. The stability ablations are also important: without plausibility filtering or bounded negative advantages, training becomes less stable, indicating that the method is not simply “add negative rewards and hope for the best.”

基于这个观察，作者提出 MTA-OPSD。核心思路是构造一个 multi-teacher pool，而不是只用一个 teacher。teacher pool 的形成方式来自对 privileged reference 的不同暴露策略，例如不同截断方式、不同 exposure ratio。这样得到一组“信息量不同、尖锐程度不同”的候选 teacher。训练时，对 student rollout 中的每个 token，不再整句共享 teacher，而是先通过 majority voting 找到相对可靠的候选子集，再用 student-teacher KL 做进一步选择，给该 token 分配一个偏好的 teacher。摘要里提到“preferred teacher always exhibits a large student-teacher KL distance”，这点有些反直觉，因为通常会担心 KL 太大意味着 teacher 太难学；作者的解释更可能是：在有多数投票约束后，较大的 KL 代表 teacher 在该位置提供了更有区分度、也更有纠偏价值的信号，而不是无意义的尖锐偏移。

与已有 adaptive OPSD 的区别有两层。第一，适配粒度从 response-level 变成 token-level。第二，选择对象不只是“参考答案暴露多少”，而是从多个 teacher 中动态选一个最适合当前位置的 teacher。方法上仍属于蒸馏框架，没有引入复杂 RL credit assignment，也没有训练额外 gating 网络；这使它实现上相对直接，但也意味着计算成本主要来自多 teacher 前向和 token 级选择逻辑。6f:T895,The paper first runs a teacher-intervention pilot study to test whether token-level teacher preference is real. The setup is simple but well targeted: keep a student-generated prefix, let a candidate teacher take over for a short continuation at a selected token position, then hand control back to the student to finish the response. The final accuracy gain of this student-teacher-student relay over pure student generation is used as a proxy for teacher suitability at that token position. This matters because it measures whether local teacher intervention actually improves the end result, rather than only comparing static distributional distances.

Motivated by that study, the authors propose Multi-teacher Adaptive On-policy Self-Distillation, or MTA-OPSD. Instead of one teacher, the method builds a pool of candidate teachers by varying how much of the privileged reference is exposed and how it is truncated. This creates teachers with different information content and different sharpness levels. During training, each token in a student rollout selects its own teacher from this pool. The selection procedure uses majority voting to identify a reliable subset of candidate teachers, followed by KL-based selection to pick the preferred teacher for that token.

The paper claims that the preferred teacher tends to have a large student-teacher KL distance. That is somewhat counterintuitive at first glance, since large KL is often associated with mismatch. The intended interpretation seems to be that, once majority voting filters out unreliable candidates, a larger KL can indicate a more informative corrective signal rather than an unhelpful overconfident one.

Relative to prior adaptive OPSD methods, the novelty has two parts. First, adaptation moves from the response level to the token level. Second, the model does not merely tune one teacher’s reference exposure; it dynamically chooses among multiple teachers for each token. The framework remains within distillation rather than RL, and it does not appear to require a separate learned gating network. The practical cost is therefore likely to come from maintaining a teacher pool and performing token-level selection.70:T67a,From the provided content, the experiments are run on mathematical reasoning benchmarks using models from the Qwen3 family. The headline result is that MTA-OPSD consistently outperforms existing OPSD baselines, with an average gain of up to +5.9 over the base model. For pretraining-focused readers, the main takeaway is the granularity of supervision matching rather than the specific math setup.72:T7df,PIVOT can be summarized as online local correction followed by student continuation, plus KL supervision on the corrected span. During training, the student first generates a rollout prefix. At a chosen intervention point, the teacher produces a correction conditioned on that student-generated prefix. The student then continues generation from the corrected context rather than from its original mistaken continuation. This produces teacher-assisted trajectories that are more likely to end in verifier-approved solutions, while still preserving part of the student’s own rollout distribution. That is a key difference from simply injecting full teacher trajectories.

The optimization has two coupled parts. First, the resulting trajectories are still optimized with the standard RLVR objective, instantiated with GRPO and verifier-based rewards. This keeps the training target anchored to task correctness rather than pure imitation. Second, a teacher-student KL loss is applied only on the correction segments, providing dense token-level supervision exactly where the teacher intervened. Instead of distilling the entire sequence, the method concentrates supervision on the local regions that are most responsible for steering the trajectory back toward a valid reasoning path.

Mechanistically, the method addresses both bottlenecks at once. Online intervention changes the rollout distribution and increases access to reward-bearing trajectories. Local KL makes those interventions learnable by turning them into parameter updates the student can reproduce later. The paper further studies practical design choices: where intervention should happen, how much teacher guidance to inject, and how the KL term should be used. A recurring conclusion is that too-early intervention risks turning training into teacher-led generation, while too-late intervention cannot rescue already broken trajectories. Either intervention alone or token supervision alone is often insufficient; the combination is the point.73:T63e,The evaluation covers two hard reasoning settings: logic games from SynLogic and mathematical reasoning benchmarks, with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution testing on the math side. The headline result is on hard logic games, where RL-only training makes limited progress: PIVOT improves mean avg@8 from 19.5% for the best baseline to 35.6%, close to a 2x gain. That is a meaningful result because it directly targets the sparse-reward regime where standard RLVR tends to stall.

The most informative ablations are not just score comparisons but mechanism tests. The authors isolate trajectory-level intervention and token-level supervision, showing that each one alone can still fail to produce strong learning. Their combination gives the strongest gains, which directly supports the paper’s framing. They also study intervention placement and the KL design, showing that teacher correction is not simply “more is better.” The intervention has to occur at a point where the student can still continue productively, while being early enough to change the probability of eventual success. On mathematical reasoning tasks, PIVOT consistently beats the evaluated baselines on both ID and OOD benchmarks, suggesting that the gains are not limited to a single synthetic logic environment.

The strongest part of the empirical section is the controlled decomposition of why the method works. The paper does more than report a better final number; it shows that changing the trajectory distribution and densifying the local learning signal solve different pieces of the RLVR failure mode.74:T5b8,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the main method figure. The key idea is the decomposition of teacher guidance into two roles: improving access to successful trajectories and making those corrections learnable at the token level. Then jump to the main results table and the ablations that compare intervention-only, supervision-only, and the combined method.

For a closer read, focus on three parts. First, the formal definition of teacher-assisted trajectories and exactly how the correction-span KL is applied; this is where PIVOT differs from full teacher rollouts or sequence-level online distillation. Second, the ablations on intervention placement and guidance strength; these contain most of the practical recipe. Third, the controlled experiments that isolate the two mechanisms. If the goal is to judge whether this can scale to larger reasoning RL settings, those experiments matter more than the headline benchmark numbers.

Two follow-up questions are worth keeping in mind while reading. One is whether intervention position and correction length could be chosen adaptively rather than by fixed rules. The other is whether the teacher must be substantially stronger than the student, or whether committee teachers or self-improving teachers could play the same role. For anyone interested in the pretrain-to-posttrain interface, the main thing to watch is the long-term tension between verifier rewards and localized KL supervision.75:T91d,The method builds on on-policy distillation and paired-model contrastive supervision. Let the student be an autoregressive policy πθ. The model first samples its own response y from prompt x, so training happens on the state distribution the student actually visits. Standard OPD would query a teacher πT on those states and train the student toward the teacher distribution, often with reverse KL. WISD replaces the external teacher with a pair derived from the same model: the original model serves as the stronger branch π+, and a weakened copy serves as the weaker branch π−. The training signal comes from their log-probability contrast on the same on-policy states, indicating which tokens the original model prefers more strongly than its weakened counterpart.

Conceptually, this is close to policy-shift supervision in DOPD-style methods. The goal is not merely to imitate a teacher distribution, but to extract a direction of improvement from the relative preferences of a model pair. This has two practical advantages. First, the supervision is dense across every token on the student’s own trajectories, which is useful for reasoning where intermediate steps matter. Second, because the strong and weak models share the same origin, the distribution gap may be easier to transfer than in privileged-information self-distillation, where the teacher is conditioned on extra context unavailable to the student.

The paper studies two training-free ways to construct the weaker model. One is low-bit quantization, which introduces systematic precision loss in the weights. The other is magnitude pruning, which removes low-magnitude parameters and reduces effective capacity. Both are cheap, require no calibration data, and can be applied directly to the original model. That design choice is important: the whole pipeline only needs unlabeled prompts.

The method relies on a meaningful assumption: the difference between the original model and its weakened copy should encode a stable capability drop, so that moving against that drop becomes a useful learning direction. Quantization and pruning are sensible choices because they induce structured degradation rather than arbitrary noise. If the weakening were too distorted, the contrast could reflect random perturbation instead of a usable improvement signal.76:T655,The experiments cover multiple reasoning architectures and scales, with benchmarks in mathematical and coding reasoning. The headline numbers are strong and broad rather than isolated. Quantization-based WISD improves average accuracy by 4.0 points and yields positive gains in 21 of 25 model–benchmark settings. Pruning-based WISD improves average accuracy by 5.5 points and yields gains in 23 of 25 settings.

The paper highlights several concrete results. With pruning, Qwen3.5-4B improves from 57.7% to 70.5% on HMMT 2025 and from 39.1% to 56.7% on LiveCodeBench v6. With quantization, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improves from 68.5% to 74.6% on HMMT 2025 and from 61.8% to 69.5% on LiveCodeBench v6. These are substantial gains for a setting that uses no privileged information.

The broader experimental story appears to test robustness across model families, task types, and weakening mechanisms, while contrasting WISD with self-distillation methods that require reference solutions or environment feedback. One practical point stands out: the weak model construction needs no calibration data, so the method is lightweight to deploy on top of an existing model.

Two caveats are worth keeping in mind while reading the results. First, the evidence is concentrated on reasoning benchmarks, so it does not automatically imply gains on open-domain chat, knowledge-heavy tasks, or long-horizon agents. Second, the true ceiling of the method likely depends on details such as trajectory quality, sampling settings, and weakening strength. Those details usually live in the ablations and appendix rather than the headline table.77:T43c,Start with the introduction and the first half of the method section. The key is to place WISD relative to three baselines: standard OPD, privileged-information self-distillation, and weak-to-strong paired-model supervision. Once that relationship is clear, the method becomes easy to parse.

Then focus on Figure 2 and the exact training objective. That is where WISD differs in substance from ordinary distillation.

If you want to reproduce it, read the appendix for hyperparameters, sampling settings, quantization bit-widths, and pruning ratios.78:T49f,CoCA samples two kinds of rollouts from the same policy: query-only responses and rubric-conditioned responses. It then compares criterion-level satisfaction across the two groups to estimate where the policy currently stands. If query-only responses already satisfy a criterion, the criterion is becoming less useful for learning. If rubric-conditioned responses satisfy it while query-only responses do not, the behavior can be elicited but has not yet been internalized. If neither group satisfies it, the criterion may be beyond the current exploration frontier. CoCA uses this diagnosis to recalibrate criterion difficulty while preserving the intended evaluation target. For policy learning, it does not rely only on scalar rubric rewards. A conditioned response is treated as a guided frontier only when it satisfies the diagnosed targets, and then it is used for token-level self-distillation. Otherwise, conditioned rollout optimization is used to expand the frontier before later distillation. Compared with standard rubric RL, the method adds criterion-level capability assessment. Compared with rubric evolution alone, it ties rubric updates to policy learning decisions.79:T435,Reinforced Adversarial Learning (RAL) is a two-player loop:
- Judge: given (x, y), learns to discriminate whether y comes from the reference set or from the current generator’s on-policy samples, producing a “probability of being reference” score.
- Generator: optimized with RL (implemented on top of Prime-RL) to maximize the judge score.
No verifiers, no rubrics, no chain-of-thought traces—only outcome-level reference answers.
The central hypothesis is an implicit curriculum: once the generator matches superficial cues (length/format/lexical style), those cues stop separating the distributions, forcing the judge to rely on deeper task-relevant structure; stronger judges and longer co-training should therefore yield better rewards and better policies.
Key contrasts:
- vs RLVR: reward is learned from examples, not computed by a checker.
- vs frozen LLM judges: the judge is trained jointly, with a moving decision boundary.
- vs demonstration distillation / trace-based adversarial training: supervision is reference answers only, not reasoning trajectories.7a:T476,Evaluated in five settings:
1) Three “verifiable but verifier-withheld” tasks: integer multiplication, code-based arithmetic-expression synthesis, and SMILES-to-formula translation. RAL with judge-only reward improves held-out correctness and in some settings matches or exceeds training with exact rewards (including variants that augment exact rewards with a generator-sized judge).
2) Two open-ended scientific generation tasks: biomedical abstract generation from in-domain references, and NIH grant abstract generation. RAL shifts outputs toward the target reference distribution without explicitly labeling the target domain, while maintaining semantic diversity; on NIH abstracts, outputs become harder to distinguish from real references for both LLM judges and human evaluators.
Ablations emphasize: judge capacity matters; longer co-training continues to improve the generator, consistent with the curriculum narrative.
(Note: the provided full-text excerpt does not include the complete result tables and exact numbers; reporting parameter counts, dataset sizes, and deltas requires the missing experimental sections/appendix.)7b:T5eb,HRS shifts distribution matching from output calibration to hidden-state editing.
1) Formulation: for each item x, predict a categorical rating distribution p(r|x) that matches the empirical human judgment distribution, covering both ordinal and nominal label spaces.
2) Oracle residual study: assuming access to human ratings, solve for an additive hidden-state correction Δh at a chosen transformer layer such that the downstream frozen layers produce a distribution closer to humans. Empirically, (i) intervening at a single layer captures most of the attainable gain, and (ii) the set of oracle corrections is largely low-rank—most improvement is preserved in a small subspace.
3) Human-Residual Steering: learn an input-conditioned intervention without human labels at test time. A small predictor g takes the layer hidden state and the original rating logits, outputs low-dimensional coefficients a, and a learned basis B maps them to Δh = B a. Apply h' = h + Δh at that layer; keep the backbone frozen while backpropagating through the frozen downstream stack into g and B.
4) Training objective: optimize proper scoring rules on individual annotations (multiple ratings per item), with objectives tailored to ordinal vs nominal judgments to encourage calibrated distribution prediction.
5) Positioning: compared to output-level calibration, HRS can express richer, input-dependent distribution reshaping; compared to distributional fine-tuning, it is far cheaper to deploy but may have a lower ceiling.7c:T449,ATI-OPD has two main components. Adaptive Teacher Intervention first samples a full response from the student and scores it with the teacher under the same prefixes. It uses a sampled-token absolute log-probability gap, related to the K3 estimator, to measure local teacher-student disagreement. The response is split into short segments, and the earliest segment whose mean gap exceeds a threshold is selected. The preceding student prefix is kept, the divergent segment and its original suffix are discarded, and the teacher writes a bounded replacement segment. The student then continues generation from this revised prefix. Adaptive Supervision Selection monitors the regenerated continuation and removes persistently divergent suffix windows from the distillation loss. This differs from length control or token reweighting because it changes the conditional trajectory before later supervision is collected. The OPD objective remains reverse-KL-style token-level distillation, implemented with teacher log-probabilities over the student’s top-16 candidates and a clipped policy surrogate.7d:T916,核心方法是定义并精确计算 leverage。给定锚点参数 θ0 和一个更新方向 Δ，作者考虑沿 αΔ 微小移动后，模型 next-token distribution 的 KL 变化。对 KL 做二阶展开，系数就是 Fisher 二次型 Δ^T F Δ，其中 F 是在固定评估语料上按 token 平均得到的 Fisher / Gauss-Newton 形式。作者不用有限差分，而是用一次 forward-mode Jacobian-vector product 精确算出每个方向的曲率 c(Δ)，再除以同一锚点、同一位移尺度下随机方向的平均曲率 c(null)，得到 leverage ρ = c(Δ)/c(null)。这样定义有几个优点：

1）它衡量的是“相对随机方向”的行为敏感度，而不是绝对 KL，因此能消掉参数重参数化和尺度的一部分影响；
2）它不需要真的沿方向 perturb 权重，因此没有有限差分在极小位移下的 cancellation floor；
3）它天然落在局部 Fisher 几何里，能把更新方向是否对准高敏感子空间这件事量化出来。

作者还定义了几种 null 和分解。isotropic null 给出标准 leverage；profile null 匹配各 tensor 的范数分布；sign-flip null 保持每个坐标的绝对值只随机化符号，用来分离“幅度放在哪些坐标”和“符号是否沿着正确协同方向”这两部分贡献。对应地，ρsign 可以理解为更新符号结构相对随机符号的价值，这在分析 DARE 随机丢弃并重缩放时尤其关键。

在实验设计上，作者既分析公开 released checkpoints，也做 controlled reruns。公开模型包括 OLMo-3、Tülu-3、Zephyr、OLMo-2 等多个阶段的 checkpoint。控制实验则在 0.5B 和 7B 规模上重跑 SFT 与 DPO，并严格使用 fp32 master weights，观察 leverage 如何随相对位移 relΔW 衰减。作者还重现 OLMo-2-1B 的 released DPO recipe，并做 recipe ablation，定位 leverage 水平来自哪些训练细节。

理论上，论文给出一个 noisy quadratic SGD 模型来解释为什么预训练窗口 leverage 会接近 1。直观上，在局部二次近似下，如果优化过程长期受梯度噪声驱动并在许多曲率方向上来回游走，那么累计位移虽然大，但在 Fisher 度量下并没有比随机方向更集中地对准高曲率子空间，因此单位位移带来的输出变化接近随机基线。7e:T9f2,实验结果很扎实，且数字有辨识度。

第一组结果是不同训练阶段的 leverage 地图。公开 checkpoint 上，预训练窗口在 prose 上基本落在 ρ≈1 的随机水平；SFT 大约在 5 左右；RL-Zero 和 RLVR 在 400 到 1,500；DPO 在 400 到 23,000。也就是说，后训练尤其 preference / RL 类阶段，虽然参数位移通常只有 10^-4 到 10^-3 或 10^-1 量级，但单位位移造成的输出分布变化远高于预训练。这个量级差跨了四个数量级。

第二组结果是 leverage 会沿训练轨迹被“花掉”。在作者控制的 SFT 和 DPO 训练中，无论 0.5B 还是 7B，只要从同一 anchor 往外走，ρ 都随着相对位移 relΔW 下降。SFT 的下降大致符合 relΔW^-0.7 到 relΔW^-1.7，DPO 则是 relΔW^-0.3 到 relΔW^-1.2。含义是：训练早期的更新方向更集中地对准高敏感子空间，越往后越接近把高 leverage 机会消耗完，后续更新的单位收益下降。

第三组结果是数值精度。若直接用 bf16 参数训练且没有 fp32 master copy，会冻结 36% 到 99% 的坐标，并使 leverage 最多下降 7 倍。更细一点，作者还发现这种设置会人为制造更新幅度与 diagonal Fisher 的对齐，而在 fp32 master 训练中这种对齐并不存在。这说明很多关于“更新偏向重要参数”的观察，可能部分是精度伪影，而不全是优化动力学本身。

第四组结果是 recipe 复现与归因。作者从 released SFT checkpoint 重跑 OLMo-2-1B 的 DPO recipe，能复现 released delta 的位移、leverage 和 sign structure。若换成一个更朴素的 recipe，在同一 anchor 上 leverage 会低 5 到 6 倍。进一步做 leave-one-component-out 控制，发现 length-normalized loss 和 batch size 128 共同抬高了 leverage 水平。这一点很有价值，因为它把“为什么某个 DPO delta 特别可复用”落到了具体 recipe 组件上。

第五组结果是 leverage 对 delta reuse 的预测。作者推导出 DARE 这类随机 drop-and-rescale 操作的相对损伤约为 (1-p)/(pρsign)，其中 p 是保留率。实测中，只要 DARE 适用，这个公式通常能在约两倍误差内预测性能损伤。说明 ρsign 确实抓住了 delta 可稀疏化、可合并的一部分核心结构。

另外，作者还对有限差分与精确 Fisher 二次型做了校验：在有限差分高于数值底噪的区域，两者在 659 个检查中有 649 个误差在 4% 以内。这给方法本身的可信度提供了很强支撑。7f:T430,This is highly relevant to pretraining research. First, it provides a stage-agnostic diagnostic that is more informative than raw loss decrease or parameter norm change. It directly measures whether an update direction is aligned with behaviorally sensitive directions in the local Fisher geometry. Second, the paper makes a strong claim: on prose, pretraining windows of 30k to 1M steps often have leverage near 1, meaning they are no more consequential than random directions of the same size. That changes how one might think about scaling, cooldown, continual pretraining, and the pretrain-to-post-train interface. Third, it elevates numerical precision from an implementation detail to a training-dynamics issue: bf16 training without fp32 master weights freezes many coordinates, lowers leverage substantially, and creates an apparent alignment between update magnitudes and diagonal Fisher that is absent in fp32-master training. Fourth, it connects leverage to delta reuse and gives a predictive handle on the damage induced by DARE-style drop-and-rescale merging.80:T950,The central object is leverage. Given an anchor checkpoint θ0 and an update direction Δ, the authors consider the KL divergence between the anchor model and the model moved slightly along αΔ. A second-order expansion gives a Fisher quadratic form, Δ^T F Δ, where F is the token-averaged Fisher or Gauss-Newton matrix on a fixed evaluation corpus. Instead of estimating this curvature by finite differences, they compute it exactly with a forward-mode Jacobian-vector product, yielding c(Δ). They then normalize by the average curvature of random directions of the same size at the same anchor, c(null), and define leverage as ρ = c(Δ) / c(null).

This construction has several advantages. It measures behavioral sensitivity relative to a random baseline rather than in absolute KL units. It avoids the cancellation floor that makes tiny finite-difference KL estimates unreliable. And it naturally asks whether an update is aligned with high-sensitivity subspaces of the local Fisher geometry.

The paper also introduces several null models and decompositions. The isotropic null gives the default leverage. The profile null matches tensor-wise norms. The sign-flip null keeps the coordinate magnitudes fixed and randomizes only the signs, which separates the contribution of where the update puts its magnitude from whether the signs are coordinated correctly. The resulting sign-structure leverage, ρsign, is especially useful for understanding sparsification and merge operations such as DARE.

Empirically, the authors combine released-checkpoint analysis with controlled reruns. They analyze checkpoints from OLMo-3, Tülu-3, Zephyr, and OLMo-2 across multiple stages. They also rerun controlled SFT and DPO at 0.5B and 7B with fp32 master weights to study how leverage decays with relative displacement. In addition, they reproduce the released OLMo-2-1B DPO recipe and ablate recipe components to identify what drives high leverage.

On the theory side, they propose a noisy quadratic SGD model to explain why long pretraining windows can end up with leverage near 1. The intuition is that under a local quadratic approximation, if SGD is dominated by noise over long horizons, the accumulated displacement can become large while failing to remain preferentially aligned with high-curvature directions. In Fisher geometry, the net direction then looks close to random.81:T8a0,The empirical picture is unusually clear. Across released checkpoints, pretraining windows sit near ρ ≈ 1 on prose, essentially at the random baseline. SFT is around 5. RL-Zero and RLVR range from about 400 to 1,500. DPO ranges from about 400 to 23,000. So post-training, especially preference- and RL-style stages, buys far more output change per unit of weight movement than pretraining does, spanning roughly four orders of magnitude.

The controlled runs show that leverage is spent along the trajectory. In both SFT and DPO, at both 0.5B and 7B, leverage decays as relative displacement grows. For SFT the decay is roughly relΔW^-0.7 to relΔW^-1.7, and for DPO roughly relΔW^-0.3 to relΔW^-1.2. The interpretation is that early updates are more aligned with behaviorally sensitive directions, while later updates consume that opportunity and become less efficient per unit displacement.

The precision experiments are especially striking. Training bf16 parameters without an fp32 master copy freezes 36% to 99% of coordinates and can reduce leverage by as much as 7x. The same setup also induces an apparent alignment between update magnitudes and the diagonal Fisher, an effect that disappears when fp32 master weights are used. This suggests that some observations about updates concentrating on important parameters may partly be numerical artifacts.

The recipe reproduction is also strong. Re-running the released OLMo-2-1B DPO recipe from the released SFT checkpoint reproduces the released delta’s displacement, leverage, and sign structure. A simpler recipe at the same anchor yields leverage that is 5x to 6x lower. Leave-one-component-out controls point to two key contributors: length-normalized loss and a batch size of 128.

Wherever DARE works, this estimate is usually within about a factor of two of the measured damage. The deeper follow-up questions are whether pretraining leverage near 1 depends on evaluating on prose, whether the same pattern holds for code or math distributions, and whether leverage could serve as an online signal for mid-training, cooldown, or continual pretraining decisions.83:T554,The theory defines a world as a finite set of states, with each modality providing an injective rendering of those states. A JEPA in each modality is trained on positive pairs whose underlying world states are sampled from a symmetric positive-pair distribution. For JEPAs with whitened second-order anti-collapse, the optimum is the spectral embedding of the positive-pair kernel. If multiple modalities share the same positive-pair distribution over world states, and the optimum is unique up to rotation, then each modality solves the same spectral embedding problem in different coordinates. Their representations therefore match up to a rotation, which the authors call the Platonic Representation Theorem. When the positive-pair distributions differ, misalignment is bounded by the mismatch between those distributions. The paper also analyzes nuisance variables: if positives preserve more of a modality-specific nuisance direction than the k-th world direction, a k-dimensional embedding will spend capacity on that nuisance, and no rotation can align it away. Good-view JEPAs use two observations of the same scene as positives; bad-view JEPAs form positives by corrupting or continuing a single observation. Next-token prediction is placed in the latter class, with prefix-continuation pairs and the softmax log-partition acting as an anti-collapse term.84:T682,The empirical results test the good-view claim across text, image, and video settings. With matched texts and encoders, good views usually produce the strongest alignment, from 145k Flickr captions to text associated with 940M web images, with both trained-from-scratch and frozen image encoders. Alignment follows a scaling law in the fraction of good views and the number of samples seen; the fitted law predicts 85 new runs with error comparable to rerunning the same configuration with another seed.
